articleTitle: Re-energization of a power system with a distribution network
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The evolving energy mix increasingly integrates variable renewable energy systems into power grids, prompting the exploration of alternative black-start approaches at the distribution network. This study focuses on the use of distributed resources connected via power electronics converters to supply loads at the distribution level through transformers, following a blackout of the transmission system. Energizing transformers generates high unbalanced inrush currents with harmonics due to iron core saturation, posing a significant challenge. Unlike synchronous machines, power electronic converters cannot support large inrush currents. This paper demonstrates a grid-forming control that provides high-quality voltage while protecting the converter by limiting the inrush current. A benchmark is then implemented to illustrate the use of grid-forming to energize multiple transformers during a distributed black-start. It also demonstrates the ability of the proposed grid-forming to synchronize with an existing grid.

articleTitle: Extension of a low-voltage laboratory grid by a grid-forming unit to perform microgrid studies
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The failure of critical infrastructures has serious consequences for the public safety of modern societies [1]. In the event of a large-scale, long-lasting blackout, these must be resupplied with electrical energy as quickly as possible. To ensure that the supply is not only dependent on the existing time-limited local emergency supply concepts, a microgrid should be built up via a decentralized energy resource (DER) at distribution grid level as soon as possible. In [2] a planning algorithm was presented as a crisis management solution for this purpose, which will be examined in a field test as part of the SiSKIN research project [3]. In preparation beforehand, the algorithm must be validated with real power flows in the Smart Grid Laboratory (SGL) at the University of Wuppertal on the Freudenberg campus [4]. To enable microgrid studies to be conducted in the SGL, a grid-forming unit had to be added, which can be used to replicate DERs in a laboratory environment.

articleTitle: Advanced power quality analytics for improved power system resilience
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: With an increase in poor Power Quality (PQ) in electricity grids, the traditional approach of painstakingly gathering and analyzing large amounts of PQ data and identifying disturbance-related insights and formulating effective mitigation—generally carried out over a period of several months—is no longer an option. This paper presents a fast, accurate, field-tested, scalable Artificial Intelligence (AI) based Power Quality Analytics (PQA) system for electricity grid resilience improvement.

articleTitle: Developing metrics to assess electric utility climate resilience
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: New York State is increasingly focused on improving climate resilience, and electric utilities are being asked to undertake considerable efforts to this effect. Unlike reliability, utilities do not have established resilience metrics to allow them to compare and track improvements in resilience over time. NYSERDA has undertaken an effort to address that need and develop two resilience metrics, one that captures preparedness, another that measures performance.

articleTitle: PoleWrap for increasing the resilience of utility poles against extreme weathers
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This paper presents the feasibility of using an in situ PoleWrap to restore the structural integrity of aged utility poles and increase their resiliency. The effectiveness of PoleWrap was evaluated through structural strengthening testing, fire testing, and field demonstrations by utility partners in US and Europe. Results show that PoleWrap not only restores the structural integrity of both wood and concrete utility poles but also increases load-bearing capacity, enhancing robustness and resiliency against extreme weather conditions such as high winds. Fire testing performance met "excellent" criteria, and field evaluations by utility partners demonstrated its effectiveness.

articleTitle: Resilient control center to substation device communication
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Resilient communication is essential for reliably exchanging parameters and measurements in distribution systems. Thus, deploying redundant hardware for both local and wide area communication, along with protocols that leverage these redundancies for automatic and timely failovers, is fundamental. This paper presents a comprehensive overview of key protocols (PRP/HSR, MPLS-TP, and MPTCP) which offer robust recovery mechanisms. Additionally, it provides a specific concept and topology that effectively combine the presented protocols to ensure resilient communication from the control center to substation devices.

articleTitle: Quantifying the resilience of sector-coupled energy systems based on potential impacts of climate change on the distribution grid
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This paper presents a method for simulating sector- coupled energy systems and quantifying their resilience for a broad range of scenarios. Using data from a German distribution grid operator, the study examines the impact of high-impact, low-probability events, such as heavy rainfall, on the power grid and evaluates the effectiveness of various mitigation measures, including Vehicle-to-Grid and Gas-to-Power systems, as well as traditional grid hardening methods. The simulation environment integrates detailed grid models to realistically assess different failure scenarios and their effects on system resilience. Results indicate that while conventional hardening methods are most effective in cost minimization, Vehicle-to-Grid mitigation measures significantly enhance resilience by mitigating initial impacts of disruptions. The study underscores the importance of sector-coupled mitigation strategies, particularly under future climate scenarios, and provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating energy system resilience.

articleTitle: Harmonics mitigation in an islandable medium voltage microgrid
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The islanded microgrid is one of the methods to improve grid resilience. Power quality in isolated medium voltage microgrids with high harmonics emitters is thus a topic that needs to be addressed in IEC standards to enable the wide use of this grid resilience tool in the future. This paper addresses the problem of power quality issues within isolated medium voltage microgrids. Today, the contractual emission limits are the “default” ones proposed in IEC standard 61000-3-6 [1] for MV customers. These values are defined assuming connection to a power system with a defined minimum short-circuit power, and they may not be suitable for microgrids supplied by a grid-forming converter. Through the analysis of a pilot project in Northen France, we propose to assess new emission limits based on the source characteristics, namely the short-circuit harmonic impedance.

articleTitle: Self-assembling microgrids for resilient distribution systems of the future
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Microgrids have emerged as a leading solution offering resilience to distribution grid operation. In the event of a power outage, microgrids can form while leveraging clean energy resources, dynamically morph boundaries, to energize the distribution system in an autonomous manner enabling self-assembly of the energized network pockets. This paper presents the concept implementation using advanced optimization techniques, validation through co- simulation, integration into a commercial DERMS platform, and a field pilot at a campus site.

articleTitle: Energy supply time in an islanded grid portion re-energized by local renewable sources
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: When a portion of the low-voltage distribution network, typically a village, is disconnected from the upstream network, due to a fault or maintenance, it can be re-energized temporarily by the distribution system operator. Usually, if closing of a normally open tie-switch connected to a neighboring feeder is not possible, a diesel generator is conveyed to the islanded grid portion, and used towards temporary energy supply. This solution though can be costly, environmentally detrimental or not available. In this paper, an alternative solution towards temporary energy supply of a islanded grid is presented, relying instead only on local renewable sources, here photovoltaic sources, and a small battery. This work further improves decision-making, by providing valuable information to system operator. Given consumption and generation time-series data, the continuous supply of the islanded grid is estimated, depending on several parameters such at the starting time and the demand response scheme enforced.

articleTitle: Increasing resilience by means of a two-dimensional transformer fleet management approach in a German utility
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Resilience of electric systems is the ability to withstand and recover from disruptions, such as technical failures, natural disasters or cyberattacks. Power transformers play a key role in this context for energy utility companies, necessitating effective management to ensure high availability, reliability, and cost-effective operation. At the same time, the current development in the energy sector, like volatile and higher loads, aged assets and long delivery times, pose a challenge for the responsible asset managers. The role of condition assessment is pivotal in ensuring the resilience of electric systems. This allows operators to prioritize investments, plan maintenance and renewal activities, enhance responsiveness to disruptions, and implement targeted measures. The ISO 55000 standard also emphasizes the role of condition assessment in asset management, enabling decision-making for maintenance and replacement strategies within the company's policy and its financial framework. However, existing diagnostic methods often provide a single value, such as a “Health Index,” lacking specificity for stakeholders responsible for fleet management from different perspectives, such as operational costs (OPEX) and investment expenditures (CAPEX). This paper presents a comprehensive approach for transformer condition assessment, utilizing a two-dimensional methodology enabling holistic optimization of the decision-making process regarding different company targets. Furthermore, it provides a possible solution for dealing with “data uncertainty”, which poses a significant challenge in condition assessment. Results from a real project involving a large power transformer fleet within a German power utility are presented to illustrate the practical implications of the new two-dimensional approach with consideration of data uncertainty. The first implementation of the approach in 2018 incorporated fleet clustering techniques and provided specific recommendations to the asset manager. Subsequently, a new condition assessment in 2022 reduces data uncertainty, allowing asset managers to evaluate previous recommendations, identify changes in transformer condition, and adjust asset management decisions accordingly. The paper emphasizes that asset management decisions derived from condition assessment and data uncertainty analysis are crucial for reducing failure risk, and consequently increasing the overall resilience of the electric systems. Furthermore, by addressing data uncertainty, asset managers can make informed decisions regarding replacement, repair measures, and proactive lifetime extension activities. The incorporation of these recommendations optimizes asset performance, extends lifetime, and ensures reliable power supply within cost constraints and risk mitigation which are key elements for a highly resilient electric system.

articleTitle: LVAC microgrid control for resilient operation: pilot results
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The ability of microgrids to support the utility depends on the control capabilities of various microgrid components and the microgrid controller. In this work, various secondary control functions required for grid code conformity in microgrids that have been tested in a pilot facility in RSE Milan, Italy, are presented. Functions tested include dispatching power to multiple battery energy storage systems (BESS), regulation curves tracking aggregate active power(P) and reactive power(Q) setpoints at the point of common coupling (PCC), and island to grid resynchronization. Resynchronizing to the main grid using ABB’s Ekip Synchrocheck module’s capabilities and using advanced control to handle differences in BESS behavior in the microgrid are shown. The pilot testing results and lessons learned are detailed in this work. Microgrids that conform to grid codes will play a critical role in ensuring the resilience of future distribution grids.

articleTitle: Experimental tests on an islanded microgrid with a diesel generator and inverter-based battery energy storage system in synchronous operation
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: In this paper, we present experimental testing conducted on an islanded microgrid featuring a diesel generator and a battery energy storage system operating synchronously. Given the microgrid’s lower inertia and short-circuit power, inverter-based resources significantly impact protection, control, and grid stability during large transients. Our field tests focus on the performance of a grid-forming battery energy storage system during abrupt disconnections of major production units, virtual inertia scenarios, and short-circuit events. The primary objective is to provide practical data for future projects involving grid-forming technology, contributing to the reliability of a decarbonized grid dominated by inverter-based resources.

articleTitle: Remote attestation by means of trusted computing in regional power grids
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Secondary substations, often located in remote areas with limited security, are vulnerable nodes in the power grid and potential entry points for attackers. To remedy these drawbacks, we propose to secure the substations by remotely attesting their hardware and software integrity. To do so, we performed a threat analysis based on the STRIDE framework, identified potential threats, and derived 38 solution requirements. In a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE), claims are collected to generate evidence as an Entity Attestation Token (EAT). Communication of the EAT between the substation and the control center is handled via IEC 61850. The control center’s verifier then analyzes the EAT to generate attestation results. The solution design is validated by a proof-of-concept (PoC) implementation featuring IEC communication (libIEC61850) between a host machine and a development board with OP-TEE and ARM TrustZone.

articleTitle: Improving smart grid resilience using unavailability analysis and maintenance optimization
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This paper presents possibilities of maintenance optimization in smart grids to enhance system resilience. First, methods for calculating unavailability of interconnected is introduced. Different modes of operation for individual system components, which may be either restored upon randomly occurring failure, or maintained using preventive actions are considered. Mathematical models for computing time dependent unavailability for both cases are presented. Subsequently, an optimization task is constructed to minimize both the system operations costs and its average unavailability for a selected mission time using multi-objective optimization methods. The entire issue is explained on a simplified model of smart grid based on real critical infrastructure. Presented results prove that efficient implementation of mathematical models of system operations can enable resolution of complex optimization problems in reasonable time.

articleTitle: A study of indirect damage prediction for electrical poles during typhoons using deep learning
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Typhoon No. 21 hit Japan in 2018, and more than 1,000 electrical poles in Kansai's distribution lines were damaged by strong winds, causing large outages. About half of the damage to electrical poles was caused by flying objects blown down by strong winds, which contacted with electrical poles and wires. Prediction of damage to distribution facilities caused by typhoons is extremely important to consider damage mitigation measures, such as reviewing design standards, making restoration plans, and preparing restoration systems and materials. In this study, a prediction model of damage to electrical poles caused by flying objects was considered to improve the accuracy of predicting damage to electrical poles caused by typhoons.

articleTitle: Generation mix scenarios benchmarking for renewable power systems: analysis and proposals
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: With the increasing focus on transitioning towards sustainable energy sources, it becomes crucial to assess various generation mix scenarios to determine their effectiveness and feasibility under a high integration of renewables. Through a detailed examination of different renewable energy combinations and their potential impact on power generation, demand, and environmental sustainability, this paper provides valuable insights for policymakers, energy planners, and stakeholders. By evaluating the performance metrics and key indicators associated with each scenario, a valuable guidance for generation mix benchmarking in the context of future renewable power systems is provided. Indeed, and apart from the models to simulate each type of power plant, it is also important to consider their integration and their relative presence in future scenarios. Moreover, the proposed mix generation benchmarking is suitable to develop and evaluate power system modeling being consistent with the current national and international roadmaps in terms of renewable integration into the grid. This contribution is also suitable to suggest general recommendations regarding the explicit generation units to be considered for power system simulations in a variety of problems, such as power flow analysis, flexibility and reliability evaluations, as well as frequency excursions and unbalanced power system evaluations.

articleTitle: Expansion of modular template framework for resilience valuation
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: EPRI’s Modular Template Framework (MTF) uses the cost of preventive behavior to quantify the cost- effectiveness, and ultimately the value of resilience, of community-scale resilience investments for specific categories of built environments (e.g., office parks, highway commercial corridors) based on the aggregated estimated cost of making individual structures resilient through the installation of battery storage; these value estimates can be applied – with appropriate normalization – to similar built environments elsewhere. Ultimately a library of value estimates (“templates”) will be developed, representing a variety of built environments. However, the MTF has limitations which compromise its usefulness as a measure for resilience valuation, as it only considers the cost of one measure to prevent service interruptions - battery storage - as a proxy for the value of resilience, and it interprets the entire value of the battery to represent resilience, though storage can provide additional value streams. Also, the MTF does not capture the broader dimensions of resilience such as community services and societal benefits. In an effort to refine the MTF, this paper will examine how to 1) extract the resilience value associated with preventive measures from other sources of value, and 2) capture the broader dimensions of resilience such as community services/societal benefits. To this end, the steps to construct an “extraction framework” for preventive measures are detailed, and the use of community resilience and societal benefit considerations to move MTF from a cost effectiveness measure to a more comprehensive valuation of resilience is discussed.

articleTitle: Problems and solutions for circulating current generation in distributed power connection
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Unlike traditional Electric Power Systems (EPS), Distributed Energy Resources (DER) are capable of being distributed and deployed near areas of power consumption on a small scale. When connected to an EPS, the transformer used for power generation from a distributed power source typically grounds the primary neutral point, unlike a transformer used for power reception. This grounding can lead to the issue of circulating currents flowing through the neutral line. Such circulating currents can cause various problems, including load imbalance due to phase-specific reverse power, phase-specific overload, and increased transformer loss. Additionally, these currents can lead to the malfunction of protective relays and generator shutdowns in the event of a power system ground fault. Therefore, this paper employs PSCAD/EMTDC (Electromagnetic Transients including DC) modeling to simulate and analyze the failures caused by excessive circulating currents flowing through the primary neutral line of the power generation transformer in distributed power connections.

articleTitle: Using machine learning for long-term forecasting of extreme weather-induced distribution grid failures
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The increasing rate and intensity of extreme weather poses a challenge to electric distribution utilities, who have historically seen high rates of outages on days with extremes. However, many utilities still prioritize investments based only on past outages, and do not account for the different effects of projected changes in extremes on different feeders. We propose a machine-learning based approach to investment prioritization that can help utilities direct investments to reduce the impacts of extremes, even if they do not have detailed asset-level data readily available. This approach involves characterizing past extremes, modeling the impacts of these extremes, and projecting the impacts of future extremes on outages across different feeders.

articleTitle: Federated learning forecasting for strengthening grid reliability and enabling markets for resilience
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: We propose a comprehensive approach to increase the reliability and resilience of future power grids rich in distributed energy resources. Our distributed scheme combines federated learning-based attack detection with a local electricity market-based attack mitigation method. We validate the scheme by applying it to a real-world distribution grid rich in solar PV. Simulation results demonstrate that the approach is feasible and can successfully mitigate the grid impacts of cyber-physical attacks.

articleTitle: Rooting for resilience: lidar and AI for utility vegetation management
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Power outages linked to extreme weather events are poised to become more common with climate change. This trend represents a growing threat to the mission of electric utility foresters and vegetation managers who serve as stewards for trees that may fall on power lines causing outages. With limited budget and staff, utilities seek to harness the power of lidar-based, AI-processed 3D digital models, which provide a comprehensive situational awareness of aboveground utility infrastructure and surrounding vegetation. One early adopter in the United Kingdom. is National Grid Electricity Distribution, which revamped its vegetation management process with lidar data in 2019: generating work orders for high priority maintenance from vegetation analytics and fixed cutting rates provided by tree contractors. Another adopter in the Midwestern United States leverages the lidar data for individual tree species and health insights to determine outage risks along the entirety of its distribution network. By embracing innovative geo- data solutions, utility companies can effectively manage vegetation and mitigate risks, ensuring the reliability and resilience of the electrical grid amidst the challenges posed by climate change.

articleTitle: A vulnerability-based approach to quantify short-term failure probabilities of MV cables and joints in presence of heat waves
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Heat waves (HW) represent a significant cause of failures in many Medium Voltage (MV) urban distribution networks in Italy. The paper proposes a vulnerability-based physics-inspired methodology to assess the short-term failure rates of the network components which are most exposed to heat waves, i.e., MV cables and joints. Such rates can then be used to estimate the rate of occurrence of multiple contingencies, thus the risk of energy not served to customers during HW events. The application of the methodology to a real event, namely the June 2019 heat wave in Italy, highlights the ability of the methodology to detect the most critical feeders. This makes the methodology suitable for application in operational planning and quasi-real time operation of the distribution grids, if fed with forecasts or real time data concerning environmental and electrical variables.

articleTitle: Risk-informed decision-making (RIDM) for enhancing energy control system reliability
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Risk-informed decision-making (RIDM) is a crucial approach used by organizations, such as NERC, NASA, FAA, FERC, and NRC, to assess and manage the risks associated with design choices. By evaluating both the probability of an event and its potential consequences, RIDM helps prioritize safety and environmental concerns. In essence, RIDM prompts questions about what could go wrong, how likely it is that it will go wrong, and what impact it might have. This paper emphasizes the value of RIDM in enhancing the reliability of safety- and protection-related energy control systems. Drawing from success stories in petrochemical and civil domains, the following key points emerge: Mitigating risk: RIDM methods have proven effective in mitigating risks during both design and operational phases. Preventing catastrophic failures: Examples of this include preventing electrically induced wildfires and cold weather outages, as identified by FERC over the past twelve years. Resilience and reliability: RIDM tools contribute to improving the resilience and reliability of new installations and modifications to existing systems, aligning with proposed modifications to the NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1. In summary, RIDM serves as a valuable framework, used by organizations regulating commercial power plants including the NRC, for informed decision-making, ensuring the health, safety, and environmental well-being of the public and our critical energy infrastructure.

articleTitle: T&D circuit segmentation for improved resilience - a case study
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Several lessons were learned from the post-analysis of the 2021 Winter Storm Uri's devasting impact on Texas' electricity grids. Among the lessons was the need for a greater granularity and flexibility by which Texas electricity utilities can shed load during emergencies, while protecting supply to critical loads. This paper summarizes the work, concepts, and findings from a transmission and distribution circuit segmentation study performed on a Texas electricity utility's system.

articleTitle: Driving programmatic reliability targets using historical outage data
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Georgia Power's Grid Investment Plan aims to improve the overall system reliability by exploring targeted improvements on several of its distribution feeders. The program utilizes several solution categories including strategic undergrounding, Basic Impulse Level improvements, sectionalizing, tie strengthening, tie additions, and new feeder additions. However, the sheer size of Georgia Power's system coupled with the budgetary limits on a program like this makes ensuring the right return on investment a necessary task. Detailed outage data that includes several key data points can help influence the solutions to invest in on the system. Developing a program of distribution reliability investments requires a large view of the system wide data and assumptions to determine the feeder list, solution category assignments, and overall budgets. However, this wide sweep approach is only the entry step to move forward. A deeper review of the feeder outages can help direct scope more clearly. First, it is confirmed that large outage events did not occur while the system was already reconfigured, artificially inflating its customer count, or masking the true location of the outage. Then, data is trimmed further to remove outages that were planned or could not be solved by typical system solutions. With this refined data, focus can be granted to specific portions of the system to ensure that the program budget is effectively dispersed to the most customers yielding true impact on the overall system reliability metrics. This paper explores how historical outage data can be leveraged to ensure that program reliability targets can be achieved within budgetary constraints by identifying outlier events, mapping the outages throughout the feeder to target highest impact areas, and ensuring that the reasons for the outages align with the solution.

articleTitle: “Through a glass, darkly” – making sense of condition / health indices
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Within the past two decades several methodologies for assessing the condition of electrical equipment and systems have evolved. These assessment methodologies produce a numerical value which is variously termed “Condition Index” or “Health Index”. Based on the value, users are advised to take preventive or remedial measures to avoid failure of the equipment and attendant unplanned outages. The various systems operate with degrees of effectiveness but are generally reactive in nature and do not provide (or at least do not make readily apparent) to the user how to proactively improve the relevant index.

articleTitle: Enhancing distribution grid resilience in era of increasingly electrified world
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The demand for electrification is rising worldwide with more use cases in e-mobility, heating, cooling, and data centers, alongside critical & noncritical traditional applications. Further, increasing dependence for, 24x7x365 uninterrupted availability of electrical energy, manifests need for resilient energy distribution infrastructure. While the integration of Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) by decentralizing energy production, is important dimension for improving overall grid resiliency from the dynamic demands & grid operation point of view, adopting resilient grid components is equally essential with presence of multiple disruptive factors. This paper after illustrating various threats affecting electrical distribution grid, highlights various technological advancements in grid components and systems design, followed by illustrations with help of real-world case studies, from actual customer installations across both developed and developing countries.

articleTitle: Evaluation of open-phase detection technologies: relay protection logics and UL 1741SB certified inverter
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Inadvertent open phase is a concern for distribution utilities due to the unregulated voltage on the opened phase, which can be caused by the distributed energy resources (DERs) and/or their interconnection transformers. IEEE Standard 1547-2018 requires the DER to detect and trip for any open-phase condition at its reference point of applicability (RPA) within 2 seconds. This paper shares the open-phase performance evaluation of an IEEE 1547-2018 / UL1741SB certified inverter, as well as a relay protection logic, under various test configurations. It is found that the inverter and the relay protection logic can detect the open-phase conditions within the 2-s standard requirement. However, there can be overvoltage concerns if the interconnection transformer is Delta (MV) / Yg (LV).

articleTitle: Improving grid resilience through transition indicators for island operation
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The development of electrical energy systems presents novel challenges for the electricity grid, including those pertaining to stability and protection. In Germany, the replacement of conventional power plants with decentralized renewable energy generation plants (RE) is underway. The majority of these plants are integrated with converters at voltage levels ≤ 110 kV. This integration enables the conceptualization of management strategies for isolated grid operation, particularly during periods of high renewable energy generation due to prevailing meteorological conditions. From an energy perspective, the transmission grid is not necessary during this time. [1] This paper investigates whether a successful transition from interconnected operation to island operation is possible. This is analyzed with the help of RMS simulations in an open source model. Various initial scenarios are specified. Finally, the results are analyzed to determine a resilience indicator that evaluates the islanding capability of the underlying distribution grid. This indicator considers the transmitted active and reactive power (vertical grid load) and the level of prevailing inertia. The aim is to demonstrate at which indicator values the grid can transition to island operation.

articleTitle: Enhancing resilience - asset monitoring and digitalization help to add DER and NOG switchgear
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: New SF6- or even fluor-gas free switchgear provides the same performance and reliability due to stringent manufacturing testing. Additional measurements inside a new switchgear or within the grid, their comparison amongst each other, using advanced analytics, provide future information and handling options. So far missing manufacturer information can be provided via an asset cantered Digital Product Passport. This will help Operator to manage Renewables integration and higher grid utilization without any compromise on grid resilience.

articleTitle: Geospatial analysis of grid resilience: assessing failure impacts, suggesting solutions, and estimating economic implications
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: In the face of escalating global energy demands and the ongoing energy transition, the pivotal role of electricity in driving socio-economic progress cannot be overstated. However, as climate risks are becoming more severe, the vulnerability of electrical grids poses a threat to communities and economies, potentially creating cascading disruptions. Addressing these challenges requires a nuanced understanding of grid vulnerabilities and strategic investments in resilience-enhancing measures. This study proposes a methodological framework to assess the resilience of transmission grids based on open-source infrastructure and spatial data. Our approach seeks to serve as a first approximation to identify localized weak spots within the grid and prioritize interventions to mitigate risks and enhance resilience. We use high-resolution population data, available transmission grid data, and open-source natural hazards maps to identify areas with both significant failure impacts and likelihood. Our findings allow for identifying recommended resilience actions in grid infrastructure, particularly in light of escalating natural hazard threats with climate change. The methodology is demonstrated on a case study for a developing country in the Caribbean, the Dominican Republic.

articleTitle: Utility seeks to improve reliability and resilience for rural customers with dynamic boundary microgrid – a feasibility study
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The surge in residential load growth in a rural area, coupled with new industrial customers possessing high reliability requirements, has stressed the existing distribution grid, leading to reliability issues for customers at the end of long, radial feeders. This feasibility study examines the potential of adopting a feeder-level microgrid solution versus new distribution or transmission lines to enhance reliability for these customers, a true non-wires alternative (NWA) project. The study focuses on optimizing reliability improvements within budget constraints, providing a thorough cost-benefit analysis of microgrid implementation. By incorporating renewable energy sources, energy storage systems, and automated controls, a microgrid can offer resilience and reliability during grid outages, and with intelligent switches it can expand its boundary based on current conditions. The analysis highlights the ability of a microgrid to provide high- quality power, reduce downtime, and accommodate future load growth effectively. The findings suggest that a well- designed microgrid not only addresses the current reliability issues but also offers long-term economic advantages and operational flexibility. This paper outlines the methodologies employed, including load forecasting, reliability assessment, microgrid siting, and financial analysis, concluding with recommended locations, distributed energy resource (DER) sizing, and switch locations for integrating microgrid into the existing infrastructure to meet the ever-evolving demands of customers.

articleTitle: Development of a web-based module for automatic electrical energy management on an animal farm for a resilient electrical system
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Guaranteeing a reliable service to consumers, while reducing power interruptions and minimising environmental impact, is one of the main challenges facing rural electricity distribution. Poor energy quality has a negative impact on production efficiency. For this reason, an automatic module controlling electrical energy from the approved distributor, solar energy and biogas, as well as internal farm parameters, has been developed to help achieve resilient energy. The device consists of an Arduino Mega board, sensors, actuators, clock and wifi modules and a web application for seamless communication between the farmer and the farm. Initial tests on the prototype revealed a minimum efficiency of 90.28% for all units. Laboratory tests showed that the module is able to communicate almost instantaneously with the farmer. It was concluded that the use of this module can seriously limit the variation of electrical energy on a farm and contribute effectively to its resilience. It therefore considerably reduces the environmental pollution caused by farms around the world and increases livestock production.

articleTitle: Enhancing electric power system resilience through modern digital protection systems
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: As organizations increasingly adopt digital trip circuits to replace legacy analog hardwired trip circuits, it is essential to recognize that these digital systems face similar vulnerabilities. The top three protection system failures identified by the Electric Reliability Organization impact digital trip circuits as well. This paper focuses on measuring the impact of modern digital protection and control systems on electric power equipment. By evaluating fault-clearing time implications, the author demonstrates asset resiliency improvements gained from high-performing, modern digital protection systems. Notable advancements, including faster phasor and time-domain protection algorithms, improved zero-crossing detection, and high-speed output contacts, contribute to faster decision-making by protective relays. These systems can even interrupt service before broken conductors fall, preventing electrically induced wildfires. The study employs standardized methods to evaluate, test, and measure digital trip circuit designs. By comparing various trip circuit latencies, the author emphasizes the importance of reliability and resilience. Additionally, the paper includes IEEE and IEC definitions of latency, providing a framework for assessing different trip circuit designs. Reliability analysis and maintenance strategies, such as IEC 60870, aid in comparing technologies. In summary, leveraging modern digital protection and control systems enhances asset resiliency, mitigates operational risks, and contributes to a safer and more reliable energy infrastructure.

articleTitle: Optimization of hydrogen-based management system for enhancing distribution network resilience
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Climate change will lead the electrical system to be increasingly vulnerable to extreme events (such as heatwaves, wildfires, storms, and floods). These events could have a negative impact on the power distribution system, causing out-of-service up to irreparable damage to lines, and equipment loss. In the paper, the value of hydrogen for improving the resilience of the distribution network in case of extreme events is assessed. A management system able to optimize the hydrogen (H2) system operation in both normal and emergency conditions is proposed. The management system can define optimal strategies that enhance network resilience by minimizing the total operation cost. Such minimization is subject to technical constraints related to H2 systems resources (i.e., electrolyzes, storage tanks, and fuel cell units) as well as their dynamic interplay. Once the critical state is known (days in advance or at short notice), the management system defines optimal H2 system resources setpoints to provide the services required to address the critical state. The proposed framework is validated by a realistic Italian rural medium voltage (MV) distribution system, focusing on one specific node within the network.

articleTitle: Resilience analysis in medium voltage distribution system: case study
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This paper presents a case study evaluating the resilience of the medium voltage distribution system in the Czech Republic. The system, which is operated in a radial or ring configuration, shows exceptional adaptability in response to a fault, effectively isolating the affected areas while maintaining uninterrupted power to connected customers. This paper presents an assessment and quantification of the impact of load break switch malfunction on the resilience of the distribution network to large-scale disturbances. Furthermore, the paper presents the possibility of considering the impact of aging of these elements on the overall system unavailability and calculating the relevant resilience metrics. The possibilities of optimizing preventive maintenance in the network to reduce the unavailability and eventual total outage-related costs are discussed.

articleTitle: Spectral analysis for tracking transient effects in distribution grids
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: In the face of the challenges posed by climate change and the rapid integration of renewable energy sources, the resilience of power distribution grids has never been more crucial. Our research introduces a novel methodology aimed at increasing grid resilience by leveraging advanced analytics enabled by simulations. We propose an algorithm to locate failures and power quality issues in the presence of modern high-power, non-linear inverter-based assets like photovoltaics (PV), battery electric vehicle (BEV) charging stations, and heat pumps. This paper explores the use of neural networks for identifying the injection point of transients and comprises two distinct experiments. Initially, we demonstrate a proof of concept using the amplitude of the third harmonic across all buses in the CIGRE-LV 44-bus distribution grid, achieving a validation accuracy of 100%. Recognizing the impracticality of full observability in real-world scenarios, we strategically reduce measurements to three buses, achieving 84.7% accuracy with a neural network. This method results in top-3 and top-5 categorical accuracies that improve to 97.3% and 98.8%, respectively, giving valuable intuition where the sources might be located.

articleTitle: Fault and protection management for a micro grid with low short circuit ratio
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This paper focuses on grid protection challenges that arise in microgrid topologies. One challenge is the coordination of protection relays, as microgrids require fault criteria that can adapt to both islanded and grid-connected modes. The other challenge is ensuring proper fault detection and isolation, given the bidirectional power flow and variable short-circuit levels linked to the increase of inverter based resources (IBR) on both low and medium voltage network.

articleTitle: On-site testing of critical components in distribution grids
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The resilience of distribution grids is contingent upon the availability and reliability of their most critical components: cables, transformers, and switchgears. It is important to recognize that resilience goes beyond the capacity to withstand unexpected external stresses. In the context of disaster recovery, the acceptance of failing and repairing grid components may be more relevant than the focus on residual lifetime or overload capability. The features of resilience present a significant technical challenge: It is crucial to determine how the health of installed equipment can be assessed after a critical event and to demonstrate that critical assets are in good condition for operation, following installation, repair or replacement. On-site testing is a well-established methodology for assessing critical assets post-installation and post-repair. Its aim is to reduce the risk of failure in the next operation cycle. In light of this, there is a growing demand for suitable on-site test systems for testing cables, transformers and switchgear. The paper will present the latest developments in this field, outlining the technical importance of selecting near power-frequency test voltages, recommended test circuits and the required test systems.

articleTitle: Distribution resiliency through FLISR implementation
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Life in today’s world revolves around mankind’s greatest engineering achievement of the 20th century, the electrical grid. Our dependency on this achievement can be unexpectedly interrupted due to a variety of reasons such as severe weather, equipment failure, vegetation growth, public interference, wildlife, or many other reasons. Regardless of the cause, a healthy and robust power distribution system should be designed to withstand and recover from these interruptions as efficiently and effectively as possible. A new focus on system capacity, robust circuit ties, hardening of existing lines, as well as adding additional isolation and switching devices will allow for the distribution grid to recover more easily and quickly from unexpected interruptions. One method currently available to mitigate these issues and provide a high level of resiliency for the power grid is a Fault Location, Isolation, and Service Restoration (FLISR) program. A FLISR program will allow the electrical grid to identify, locate, and isolate the portion of the damaged grid that disrupted service, while at the same time, allowing the grid to automatically restore power to the undamaged sections. The FLISR system utilizes data communicated from electronic devices on the distribution system to quickly calculate and determine the best response needed to isolate the issue and restore power through robust connections to unaffected portions of the grid. As reclosers and fault indicators are deployed across the grid, FLISR will be able to utilize this information to pinpoint locations of faults and damage with a speed and accuracy previously unseen on the distribution system. Not only will FLISR automate the restoration of customers from adjacent tie circuits, but it will also assist utility operations in identify steps to perform localized manual switching before repairs begin to allow the grid to recover from interruptions. This system provides an enhanced level of resiliency compared to how the electrical grid previously operated throughout the 20th century. Implementation of such a program raises serious challenges and opportunities for electric utilities including program cost, engineering design, and operational safety. Raising customer rates to pay for programs such as FLISR has never been more difficult. Regulatory bodies and consumer advocates are increasingly prepared to argue against any type of rate increases. Any utility interested in implementing a FLISR program needs to have a well thought out strategy that effectively identifies the risks and opportunities as well as how that program will benefit customers and potentially drive costs down elsewhere. Concerns about safety to both the company’s personnel and the public are real and valid. A utility must consider the operational impact and implications of an automated FLISR system to realize its benefits while at the same time protecting its workers and the public from harm. The engineering design of the FLISR system must be thorough and precise. If mistakes are made in the configuration and programming of the system, promises of increased resiliency and reliability can easily turn into a drop in those same metrics. To effectively capitalize on the opportunities of a FLISR program while reducing its risks, utilities, coops, and municipalities need to develop a robust strategy that correctly assesses the current state of their grid, as well as how to best prepare their great engineering achievement for the next generation of robust and resilient performance.

articleTitle: Hybrid load restoration for hierarchically controlled microgrids
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The increasing penetration of distributed energy resources (DERs) results in fast and large dynamic responses in microgrids during load restoration service due to low inertia and complex controls. To address this challenge, this paper devises a hybrid load restoration algorithm for hierarchically controlled microgrids to provide a frequency/voltage dynamics-constrained restoration service. Our contributions include: 1) a hierarchical control-integrated load restoration model for microgrids, considering power sharing and voltage regulation effects; 2) dynamics-coupling constraints explicitly integrated the impacts of frequency and voltage dynamic responses into the restoration optimization model; 3) a hybrid microgrid load restoration framework which integrates a mixed integer linear programming (MILP)-based optimization model and a dynamic simulation. Numerical simulations carried out on a typical 33-bus microgrid reveal the effectiveness of the hierarchically controlled microgrid load restoration under different scenarios.

articleTitle: GIS-based approach to improve the resilience of the distribution network
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The subject addressed in this work is the role of resilience in planning distribution networks. Resilience understood as the ability to anticipate, operate, and learn from disruptive events, is emerging as a fundamental principle in the planning and operation of networks. This work introduces a GIS-based approach to tackle the issue of resilience in network planning. The specific circumstances notably influence the disruptive events that may affect the network. Therefore, a resilience approach must effectively manage both the system’s technical characteristics and the particularities of its location. Geographical Information Systems (GIS) allow the management and analysis of large amounts of geolocated data. The GIS-based approach proposed in this work addresses the system’s resilience considering hazards, defined as disruptive events that may impact the infrastructure without being controllable, and vulnerabilities, described as infrastructure weaknesses characterized by their likelihood of occurrence when a hazard is present and the potential impact they may cause.

articleTitle: Holistic resilience monitoring in state-of-the-art power supply systems
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events, the growing share of renewable energy resources, as well as an advancing digitization brings along new vulnerabilities and opportunities to the complex power supply system. The classical risk assessment is not sufficient to prepare for these developments. A resilience assessment identifies vulnerabilities through an encompassing system analysis, which allows to quantify the resilience of the system. The holistic monitoring of this system resilience in real-time is a key aspect of a such an assessment. A prototype of a so-called resilience monitor will be presented in this paper, and its operation is sketched for two use-cases. Besides depicting the current system resilience, it can further provide recommended actions based on the evaluation of key performance indicators. The encompassing resilience monitoring of any system requires a comprehensive set of data. Due to the notorious lack of such data, we reduced the demonstration of the monitor operation to the key aspect of island capability in both use-cases, for which data could be sufficiently collected by the respective monitor users themselves.

articleTitle: Resilience-oriented planning of distribution networks with a two-stage approach
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This paper proposes a two-stage methodology for distribution network resilience appraisal. The first stage evaluates the current and the expected future resilience of a distribution network that serves a large portion of the territory on which many distribution networks are located. The second step delves into the study of the resilience of those networks identified as the most critical in the first step. The paper proposes a comprehensive application of the approach to a real-scale distribution system to demonstrate its use for planning resilient distribution networks of the future.

articleTitle: A data-driven approach to assessing Brazilian power grid's resilience to extreme weather events
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events pose significant challenges to the resilience of Brazilian electricity distribution systems. This study presents a data-driven approach to evaluate the resilience of the Brazilian power grid, focusing on high-impact, low- frequency (HILF) events such as cyclones, tornadoes, torrential rains, wildfires, and floods. By analyzing outage data from 2018 to 2023, we extracted the network's response to extreme events, including the number of consumers affected, the duration of outages, and the standard deviation of the system restoration. Additionally, we applied survival function analysis to estimate the probability of prolonged outages and system recovery times, offering actionable insights for resource allocation. This research provides valuable statistical information to enhance contingency planning and improve the overall resilience of electricity distribution systems to future extreme weather event.

articleTitle: Automated tightly-stacked protection coordination
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Segmentation of distribution feeders reduces the number of customers affected by faults. During extreme weather events, multiple faults can occur in a very short period of time, and it can take significantly more time for repair crew to address all of them. This makes segmentation critical particularly during storms. Keeping more customers connected, and especially distributed generation that can be critical in restoring neighboring sections of the network, contributes significantly to the resiliency of the system to severe (major) weather events. This paper introduces a novel method of coordination that reduces engineering effort, allows for greater segmentation, and improves the speed of fault clearing operations.

articleTitle: Modeling damage cascades in critical infrastructure for power outages
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This paper shows a network modeling approach which encompasses a diverse set of critical infrastructures and their mutual dependencies. It can be employed to analyze and quantify the effects of various disasters, e.g., large-scale, long-lasting power outages. The approach simulates damage cascades based on the numerous interdependencies between the CIs, i.e., the temporal evolution of the system breakdown is evaluated. As an application, the effects of power outages on network models for two regions in Germany are inspected.

articleTitle: Advanced resilience planning for distribution systems
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Climate change has led to an increase in the frequency and severity of extreme weather events, posing significant challenges for power distribution systems. In response, this work presents a planning approach in order to enhance the resilience of distribution systems against climatic hazards. The framework systematically addresses uncertainties during extreme events, including weather variability and line damage. Key strategies include line hardening, backup diesel generators, and sectionalizers to strengthen resilience. We model spatio-temporal dynamics and costs through a hybrid model integrating stochastic processes with deterministic elements. A two-stage stochastic mixed-integer linear approach is developed to optimize resilience investments against load loss, generator operations, and repairs. Case studies on the IEEE 15-bus benchmark system and a realistic distribution grid model in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia demonstrate enhanced system robustness as well as cost efficiency of 10% and 15%, respectively.

articleTitle: Grid-wide distribution resilience planning framework
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Resilience planning is a strategic assessment new to most utilities. There is currently no standardized or widely adopted framework to study distribution grid resilience from a planning perspective. Many studies of grid-wide resilience rely on measured past performance, but those studies are limited to the events that have occurred, the portion of the grid that has been impacted, and the grid conditions prior to any restoration that has occurred. Therefore, measured resilience is not a proper indication of future grid-wide resilience. This paper describes a planning framework, developed in collaboration with 28 distribution utilities, to quantify distribution grid-wide resilience.

articleTitle: Design and technology innovation to meet the resilient requirements of the evolving sub-transmission and distribution network
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The population growth, industrial development, community urbanization and transport electrification are already placing significant strain on the existing electrical network. The extension of proven usage of high- temperature low-sag (HTLS) conductors from the transmission system to the downstream with innovative and economical conductor fitting designs can facilitate the upgrade of aging infrastructure in sub-transmission (34.5~69kV) and distribution systems. The results of laboratory experiments and the practical deployment of this technology in utility network demonstrate improved performance, greater resilience, and more sustainable methods for modernizing distribution network.

articleTitle: Power system resilience and enhancement assessment for volcanic risk in Taranaki, New Zealand
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This study presents a volcanic resilience assessment for the electricity network in Taranaki, New Zealand, modelling the distribution system as a standalone Critical Infrastructure (CI) and incorporating key interfaces such as transmission Grid Exit Points and generator nodes. Previous volcanic risk assessment studies have identified potentially severe impacts on the electricity infrastructure, but have not included power flow analysis. This research addresses this gap and applies natural hazard risk assessment approaches and power system resilience analysis to assess system level impacts for a complex multi-hazard volcanic hazard scenario. The impact is estimated through power flow calculations and Monte Carlo-based outage analysis.

articleTitle: Resilient features of a grid-forming multiport power converter
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Multiport power converters offer a conversion solution with improved efficiency and energy management. Grid-forming controllers can operate in weak and islanded grids. This paper introduces a grid-forming multiport power converter to support distribution network resilience, highlighting its key hard- and software features.

articleTitle: CoMap project: integration of grid analyzers in digital twins for improved grid monitoring and resilience
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The energy sector in Germany and worldwide faces new challenges in supply security, efficiency, and reliability due to the recent transformation and expansion of renewable energies. Consequently, digitalization of the existing and expanding grids has become essential for grid operators to ensure a stable and steady power supply to customers. These complex systems and their challenges can be analyzed and studied using modern development methods such as digital twins. This paper presents the CoMap project, which aims to enhance the analysis capabilities of control room systems for distribution grid operators by integrating grid analyzers into digital twins using a real-time simulator. Through the CoMap project, an ecosystem of devices and applications is provided, enabling grid operators to meet the stringent requirements of climate goals imposed by government and international regulatory agencies.

articleTitle: Quantifying resilience enhancing system parameters for electrical low and medium-voltage grids
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: In power system engineering the concept of resilience has critical importance because a resiliently designed system can save lives, reduce costs, and mitigate the overall negative impact of shocks. This paper addresses the quantification of resilience through a holistic approach that includes both the network topology and properties that contribute to strengthening resilience and flexibility or reducing vulnerability. A metric for resilience quantification has been developed, encompassing system properties such as diversity, connectivity, subsidiarity, redundancy, and storage capabilities. The proposed resilience assessment method is tested on various electricity networks.

articleTitle: Evaluating overhead distribution structure resilience through full-scale testing
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Utilities maintain a vast amount of aging infrastructure that is exposed to severe weather. Overhead structures are susceptible to storm damage from high winds and falling trees and limbs. The degree and location of damage is difficult to predict. Utilities have designed structures to support equipment, wind, and ice. However, falling trees and large branches can apply extreme loads that exceed design criteria. Structural damage during these events can lead to outages, and the outage duration is dependent on the type and extent of the structural damage that occurs (Figure 1). The Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) has collected data to enable structure design focused on faster restoration in the event of damage. EPRI has investigated the structural performance of overhead assets through extensive mechanical load testing. Testing approaches have included static and dynamic load testing of components and assemblies, including dynamic tests of full-scale distribution lines built to utility standards and specifications. This data has enabled mechanical coordination of components to hasten restoration times by isolating structural damage to failure modes that take less time to repair. For example, a broken conductor tie reduces the transfer of energy to the top of the utility pole and reduces the likelihood that the pole will break. Crews can repair this damage quickly, but broken poles are associated with long restoration times. This paper summarizes a selection of research performed by EPRI and demonstrates how mechanical coordination can improve resilience. It introduces a framework to quantify the resilience of a structure based on its performance in a full- scale test and demonstrates the implementation of that framework on two utility-created designs.

articleTitle: LVDC distribution system for long distance in mountainous areas for resilience enhancement
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This study introduces a new low-voltage direct current (LVDC) distribution method aimed at improving the reliability of power supply in mountainous areas susceptible to Natural disasters. Incorporating converters for AC to DC750V conversion and power flow control through multiple batteries, the proposed distribution method demonstrates higher resilience and compatibility with distributed power sources, such as photovoltaics (PVs) and electric vehicles (EVs), compared to conventional AC systems. This paper discusses the system's configuration, control methods for steady and transient states, and verification through simulation and demonstration circuits, presenting results that highlight the system's ability to mitigate voltage drops and maintain stable power supply during load fluctuations. Future research will focus on optimizing control during reverse power flow, conducting verifications at a DC 750V level, and exploring economic benefits of utilizing existing AC infrastructure.

articleTitle: Co-simulation and small-signal analysis tool for multiple DER integration studies
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The aim of this paper is to present a co-simulation and small-signal analysis tool. The objective of the co-simulation tool is to provide a way of evaluating DER contribution to improve the resiliency of the distribution grid, both in MV and LV, when multiple DER are connected to it. The tool provides an environment to assess the impact of different choices for DER allocation, as well as functionality to identify potential threats to grid stability. This is achieved by inspecting the results of yearly simulations on the power flow or by identifying critical modes from the small-signal model of the grid.

articleTitle: Energy modi: transactive grid management scheme for resilient micro-grids
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The adoption of renewables leads to an intermittent peak supply of energy during certain parts of the day which results in congestion in the distribution grid and energy scarcity scenarios for community micro-grids in other periods of the day. In this paper, we present a transactive mitigation scheme based on multi-objective steering signals shared between different grid entities to solve gird issues, with a focus on congestion. We evaluate the proposed approach using baseload data from 25 houses in New York by simulating a congestion scenario resulting from cost minimization optimization. We show that the proposed congestion mitigation approach resolves the congestion with minimal sacrifice of the comfort of the residents of the micro-grid.

articleTitle: Physical-informed machine learning framework for outage prediction against high impact events to enhance grid resilience
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This paper introduces a novel physics-informed machine learning (PIML) framework aimed at enhancing the accuracy of outage prediction models (OPMs) for electric utilities, particularly during high impact weather events exacerbated by climate change. The proposed PIML framework incorporates physical grid infrastructure attributes into machine learning models, addressing traditional machine learning model shortcomings by ensuring good data quality, model robustness, and reliability. The implementation on the Puerto Rico grid system demonstrated the PIML model's superior reliability and accuracy in predicting outages, providing utilities with an effective tool for strategizing grid hardening measures. This advancement supports better preparation for high-impact events and contributes to broader efforts in enhancing grid resilience and service continuity under changing climatic conditions.

articleTitle: Reliable 5G network slicing for distributed energy systems: validation of live performance during high-load event
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The shift towards renewable energy sources is accompanied by increased use of decentralized monitoring and control systems for handling, e.g., distributed energy resources (DERs). In turn, this requires pervasive and reliable communication throughout all levels of the energy grid. Here, traditional approaches need dedicated infrastructures to enable robust and scalable Information and Communication Technologies (ICT). However, the fifth generation of mobile radio networks (5G) enables telecommunication providers to provision virtually dedicated and thus isolated network slices to user equipment, enabling mixed-critical communications of energy devices via existing public infrastructure. Within this work, we present real-world performance measurements of a live network slice during a high-load scenario, thereby illustrating the current state of commercial network slicing solutions as well as providing an outlook on ongoing research.

articleTitle: Multi-assessment tool for electric distribution systems
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The electrical distribution grid is essential for societal infrastructure. Any disruption to the system can have significant social, economic, and political consequences. Ensuring its resilience by anticipating potential issues is critical. This study introduces a multi-assessment tool designed to analyze and enhance the resilience of the distribution grid by performing comprehensive risk assessments. The tool collects and stores data from various sources, utilizing a range of algorithms from simple calculations to advanced artificial intelligence. It integrates geographic data for visualization through GeoServer and MapStore, enabling users to add maps and layers relevant to the electrical configuration and to generate tables and graphs for monitoring. The tool incorporates meteorological data to assess impacts on the grid, setting thresholds to identify vulnerable areas. An algorithm locates electrical faults and suggests grid reconfigurations to minimize consumer impact, employing machine learning for rapid fault detection. Additionally, it calculates dynamic thermal rating (DTR) and distance between the towers and the lowest point of a conductor (sag) for aerial lines to ensure safe operation. This georeferenced web service, built on open-source platforms, integrates various aspects of the electrical system, enhancing its resilience and vulnerability assessment. The tool's ability to connect with third-party sources underscores its flexibility and effectiveness in real-world applications.

articleTitle: Influence of extreme temperatures on the lifespan of power transformers and cables in Benin’s electricity distribution network by 2035-2050: innovative approach for sustainable improvement of resilience
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The article aims to contribute to a better understanding of the aging of transformers and the weathering profile of the cables of the electricity distribution network in Benin in the context of climate change. Probabilistic modelling of transformer life i s performed associated with the use of a phenomenological model based on thermoelectric stresses. The results obtained indicate that in long-term standby mode with a temperature of the hot spot (the transformer consumes on average 82 days/ year of its life, and the average life of the electric cables is between 18 and 28 years, aggravating the current vulnerability of the Beninese electricity grid with a rate likely to deteriorate from 36% to 50% by 2035 perspectives 2050. To improve resilience, an innov ative approach based on real-time hot spot temperature monitoring of power transformers and cables, from smart sensors and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies and or SCADA on the perimeter of the departure of Fidjrossè in Cotonou in Benin is studied. It strengthens the resilience of the distribution network and facilitates its restoration in real time in case of avalanches.

articleTitle: Electrical resilience: adaptation to the volcanic eruption in La Palma
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Following the volcanic eruption on the island of La Palma, continuous gaseous emissions have significantly altered the environmental conditions, increasing atmospheric corrosivity and deteriorating metal elements, ceramic insulators, and power transmission cables. This study reproduces ash deposition in a laboratory setting and conducts electrical and corrosion resistance tests on affected materials. Characterization of volcanic ash confirmed heightened environmental corrosivity due to sulphur emissions, monitored through corrosion control coupons placed near the volcano. To evaluate flashover phenomena in insulators, it has been simulated volcano ash deposition on it and performed electrical behaviour tests. The findings provide a comprehensive view of the corrosion challenges faced by electrical substations in volcanic environments. The study also presents innovative mitigation strategies to enhance the reliability and resilience of electrical systems under adverse conditions.

articleTitle: Active multipath pseudowire ensures uninterrupted communications for line differential protection
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Line differential protection (87L) systems have stringent network requirements that include low latency, symmetric delay, jitter mitigation and rapid failure recovery. This paper explores how IP/MPLS networks can provide highly reliable communications for these critical systems through advanced capabilities such as deterministic quality of service (QoS), flexible playout buffers, asymmetrical delay control and an innovative redundancy protection scheme called active multipath pseudowire. The paper examines key challenges and describes tailored IP/MPLS capabilities for addressing latency, jitter, delay symmetry and hitless recovery needs. It introduces an active multipath mechanism that extends pseudowire redundancy by replicating traffic over multiple active paths to enable hitless recovery and multi-fault resilience. The paper also includes the results of an industry validation effort that demonstrates how modern IP/MPLS networks can deliver the utmost reliability and availability required for line differential protection, ensuring grid resiliency and availability.

articleTitle: Study about the improvement asset reliability and utilization by re-establishing the replacement criteria for transformers using AMS
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: KEPCO is using the NDIS system to select the transformer maintenance target.
