Instead of measuring the load information of the transformer installed in the power distribution line as it is, monthly usage is collected through the power meter and applied as the load of the modulator connected to NDIS. When selecting the target for replacing KEPCO's overload transformer, the actual load should be re-measured in accordance with the transformer management standards by considering the load amount by NDIS side, and the actual overload transformer should be replaced. The problem is that the actual load measurement time does not match the time when the maximum load is generated in summer or winter, making it impossible to measure overload in reality. In addition, old transformers are also selecting replacement targets using various replacement criteria through H.I. In particular, it is positive that civic accidents were prevented by newly reflecting the HI score for the installation of the instantaneous pressure reduction device, but the fact that it has a great influence when selecting a replacement target for old transformers implies the need for improvement. Therefore, this paper compares and analyzes the overload transformer replacement target selection method of some workplaces, the HI-based old transformer selection method, and the transformer selection method using AMS, and suggests improvement directions for current transformer management standards.

articleTitle: Results from lab testing of vanadium redox flow battery
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Increases in occurrences of utility power outages due to weather related events and the potential for cybersecurity threats have created new challenges to ensuring resilient installation operation. Microgrids allow installations to maintain continuity of service and continue to serve critical loads for long duration outages. Traditional batteries in microgrids typically complement diesel generation (DG) operation as opposed to DG replacement, primarily because of the high cost and limited energy duration of commercially available battery technologies. Flow battery technology offers a potential alternative to traditional chemistries to reduce dependence on DGs while still ensuring system reliability. Vanadium Redox Flow Batteries (VRFB) offer unique differentiators to lead acid and lithium-ion battery technologies such as increased safety, longer rated duration, and longer life. However, the nascency of VRFB technology and limited understanding of reliability and operational performance, coupled with high equipment cost, typically limit the opportunities for field deployment. This paper characterizes the reliability and ability of VRFB technology to support a microgrid.

articleTitle: Dynamic power quality monitoring via power decomposition
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Renewable energy resources with inverter-based technologies are advancing rapidly, producing more efficient and environmentally sustainable energy. However, these technologies introduce technical challenges for electric utilities, particularly concerning power quality issues. This paper presents advanced power quality (PQ) event detection within Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) using high-bandwidth, precise sensors and advanced power quality meters. A utility test bed was monitored, revealing an event with power quality disturbances. We employ dynamic phasors to represent polyphase voltage and current waveforms, focusing on power decompositions that combine these signals. This approach yields more interpretable quantities, serving as reliable signatures for detecting and classifying various PQ events.

articleTitle: A novel resilience tool and its application to Senegal's power system
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: In response to the escalating frequency of severe weather events induced by climate change and their impact on power systems, the Energy System Consulting division of Tractebel Engineering GmbH’s R&D team has developed a unique tool, reXplan. ReXplan is designed for resilient electrical system planning in the context of extreme hazards such as windstorms, earthquakes, floods, wildfires, and more. This paper will first present the tool’s main characteristics and specificities before diving into a specific case study conducted in collaboration with the World Bank, focusing on the application of reXplan to Senegal’s power system.

articleTitle: Laboratory test to validate concepts to build up and operate a microgrid at distribution grid level after a blackout
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: After a blackout, critical infrastructures can be resupplied by a microgrid at distribution grid level [1]. This microgrid has to be build up from a black start capable grid-forming power plant, which is also located at distribution grid level. To avoid overloading of the microgrid, it has to be interconnected step by step, otherwise it might collapse again [2]. A grid-forming power plant can use a generator or an inverter to build up a microgrid. Typically, grid-forming power plants at distribution grid level, such as hydropower plants or waste-to-energy plants, use generators. With future expansion of technologies such as fuel cell or battery storage, inverter-dominated technologies will be located at distribution grid level. With a grid-forming inverter, a microgrid can be build up at distribution grid level. In a previous paper, three concepts were presented to build up a microgrid using a grid-forming inverter [3]. This paper demonstrates the practical implementation of these concepts in a real low-voltage grid, where a grid-forming inverter is used. First, the three concepts are outlined, beginning with the approach where a grid-forming inverter builds up the microgrid and controls frequency and voltage. It is shown how the grid-forming inverter can be supported by additional feeding power plants, which are reachable by blackout-proofed telecommunication. The second concept presents the buildup of a microgrid with a droop-controlled grid-forming inverter and droop-controlled feeding power plants, where no blackout-proof communication is required. The last concept contains the buildup of a microgrid utilizing an overlaid controller. The controller manages the grid-forming inverter and all feeding power plants of the microgrid. Due to the controlled setpoints of the feed-in power, power plants with secured feed-in power can take heavier loads compared to power plants with high volatility.

articleTitle: Resilience-aware allocation and dispatch of distributed BESS in microgrid structured RES-based grids
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Battery energy storage systems (BESSs) are essential in future grids. Being less constrained by location, distributed BESSs (D-BESSs) can be installed near the demand to enhance resilience. When D-BESSs are considered during the network planning phase, distribution and transmission networks resilience can be enhanced with minimum or no additional cost as this paper explains. A key enabler for harnessing the benefit of these D-BESSs is to effectively manage their operation through distributed control architecture where local microgrid controllers can provide significant support. In this paper, a scheme to size, dispatch, and control D-BESSs is proposed such that the associated use cases of these resources can effectively be attained to support the stable operation of future power grids.

articleTitle: Directional zero sequence active power algorithm for resonant earthed networks
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Over the past few years, Rapid Earth Fault Current Limiter (REFCL) technology has been widely deployed on the electricity distribution grid in Victoria, Australia. This uses an Arc Suppression Coil (ASC) to form a resonant earthed network, along with substation-based power electronics to minimise the voltage on the faulted phase to near zero. But with REFCL systems seeking to eliminate fault currents, there is a lack of selectivity and sensitivity by zero-sequence protective relays and recloser controls on the feeders. This paper will detail a novel method of detecting the direction of the fault transient by using a zero-sequence active-power sectionaliser element in the advanced recloser devices a utility installed. This methodology, coupled with accurate phase-current sensors in the advanced reclosers’ Rogowski coils, is shown to successfully provide directionality. This paper also will detail how the proposed algorithm fared when tested against pre-recorded waveform data from field events during algorithm validation. It then presents field results from controlled primary earth faults using a test trailer. Finally, this paper will detail field results from uncontrolled fault events over a broad range of high and low fault impedances.

articleTitle: Eco-friendly IoT switchgear – reducing uncertainty while accelerating SF6-free transition
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: In many industries, the practice of involving end-users early in the product development cycle has proven highly effective. However, this approach is only now gaining traction in the traditionally conservative power industry, where utilities have historically prioritized reliability and risk aversion. This paper explores the principles, benefits, and implementation of "Alpha Projects"—a methodology aimed at accelerating innovation by working directly with users to test new technologies in their early development stages. This strategy allows both manufacturers and utilities to reap significant benefits through close collaboration and real-time feedback. It also means that both parties are willing to take some calculated risk since Alpha products are not fully vetted and suitable for 30-year life in harsh conditions. As part of this initiative, an SF6-free gas switchgear has been deployed in the field with several sensors to monitor its health status for 12 months.

articleTitle: Extensive meshed network resilience analysis
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The paper deals with the resilience analysis of a real, extensive meshed MV/LV network. The scope of the analysis is the resilience of this network to multiple MV feeders outages and consequential cascading failures. The resilience is evaluated with regard to preserved load in the network. The case study focuses on cascading failures of selected outage combinations with four lost feeders. Based on simulation results weakest elements in the network are identified. Furthermore, measures for resilience enhancement are presented and discussed.

articleTitle: Enhancing asset management for improved resilience through representative generation profiles
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The increasing integration of grid rooftop photovoltaics into low voltage networks is requiring a meticulous review of methods used for asset management in power systems. Particularly, the suitable assessment of the reverse power that flows through distribution system assets has become challenging due to uncertainties in the availability of solar resources and energy consumption patterns. Furthermore, the diverse accessibility of solar resources in the utility concession area highlights the need for efficient methods to identify regions with similar solar potential, crucial for accurate management of the aging infrastructure. Thus, this paper addresses these challenges by proposing the adoption of representative power generation profiles to estimate the power output of photovoltaics installed in a given region, supporting more effective planning and asset management strategies to improve the resilience of the current power systems.

articleTitle: Compensate renewable energy producers for periods when local constraints do not allow them to inject using the linear regression
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The topic addresses the development and application of a machine learning-based method by Enedis. As the main French distribution system operator, Enedis predicts renewable energy power plants load profiles to alleviate local network constraints coping with load reduction. Load reduction limits stress on source substations during peak production periods. Enedis proposes a solution to measure the impact of the load reduction using information from others nearby renewable power plants not impacted by load reductions.

articleTitle: Using advanced analytics and artificial intelligence to improve resilience: distribution network topology and loss identification
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The landscape of distribution network management is rapidly evolving, driven by the necessity to enhance efficiency, reliability, and sustainability in energy delivery. Traditional methods of network management are increasingly being challenged by the complexities and demands of modern energy consumption and Distributed Energy Resources (DER) patterns. Inaccurate asset databases, uncharted cable paths, and connection discrepancies are just a few of the persistent issues that hinder effective network management and lead to significant and unidentifiable energy losses. In this dynamic field of distribution network management, the adoption of digitalization stands as a pivotal strategy to overcome prevalent challenges in planning and maintenance. This paper introduces a strategy to meticulously identify the network topology and accurately pinpoint losses, both technical and fraudulent, through the use of a single product. This solution, based on a set of portable, easy-to-install current recording devices and AI algorithms that run on a user-friendly platform, achieves the identification of customer connections (including LV and MV distribution network transformers, phase, and feeder) pinpointing various losses within that network. Emphasizing the critical need for detailed network topology, this study highlights its significance in creating accurate digital twins, improving grid monitoring, and finding loss origins. This concerted topology identification endeavor aims to generate a dependable and intricately detailed distribution network map offering numerous advantages. An accurate topology database is the fundamental pillar for the digital twin, which not only simplifies the integration of DERs, Electric Vehicles (EVs), and HVAC systems, thereby augmenting the network's capacity and resilience but also enables utilities to calculate network balance, identify the origin of quality issues, and identify power loss, facilitating targeted corrective measures.

articleTitle: URI winter storm impact on the Texas electricity grid & lessons learned - a review
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This paper reviews the prevailing conditions before and after the 2021 Winter Storm Uri (WSU), related lessons learned for the industry, and actions taken by the State of Texas' legislature, the Public Utility Commission of Texas' (PUCT), and ERCOT's response to those lessons. The paper also covers salient aspects of the Texas Legislature House Bill 1500, known as the Public Utility Commission (PUC) Sunset Bill, which came into effect following the lessons learned from the WSU and has a wide-ranging impact on the electricity utility regulation and administration in Texas. Furthermore, the paper also reviews the PUCT's approved blueprint for the wholesale electric market design and directives for ERCOT.

articleTitle: Analysing level of harmonics in MV-networks to enhance newly designed function for real-time monitoring of residual current level in dispatch system
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Increased capacitive earth fault currents due to the high level of cabling significantly increased demands for the safe and reliable operation of compensated networks. A high value of capacitive currents currently leads to an unknown alteration of residual current since the value of residual current is not being monitored in the dispatch system. The residual current serves as an essential parameter for estimating the touch and step voltage in the event of an earth fault and designing earthing systems. The results of the extended analysis proved that the present method for determining the residual current is no longer sufficient for ensuring the safe design of earthing systems. Thus, a new method for estimating the residual current is proposed based on the newly designed function that is embedded in the regulator of the arc-suppression coil. The new function presents an opportunity for real-time monitoring, even predicting, the estimated value of residual current in the dispatch system. However, the regulator of the arc-suppression coil can only calculate the value of the residual current for fundamental frequency, which does not comply with standards. Higher harmonics must be included in the designed function to estimate the real residual current. The main aim of this research paper is to present the results of an analysis that was conducted to determine the level of higher harmonics of residual current that were measured in the various compensated networks. The emphasis is also put on the possible automatization of the designed function for real-time monitoring of the residual current level in the dispatch system while considering possible situations that might happen in real distribution networks.

articleTitle: Multiport power converters to enhance resilience in distribution networks
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The distribution grid is undergoing a transformation due to the rise in renewable energy generation. The variability in energy production or the lack of inertia resulting from the displacement of synchronous generators could have a significant impact on grid resilience. Therefore, solutions for reliable green energy generation are required. Multiport Converters are presented in this work as a suitable alternative. In particular, a Multiport Converter structure is presented that guarantees reliable distribution network operation in the presence of various abnormal conditions such as faults or islanding.

articleTitle: Integrative modelling and resilience enhancement in critical infrastructure systems: a comprehensive approach
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The increasing complexity and interconnectedness of critical infrastructure systems necessitate advanced analytical capabilities for effective management and resilience enhancement. This paper addresses the inadequacy of traditional modelling tools in handling the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of modern infrastructures, focusing on power distribution networks, communication networks, and control systems. We propose an integrative modelling approach that combines system dynamics, agent-based modelling, and probabilistic risk assessments, supported by real-time data analytics and machine learning. This methodology enables comprehensive simulation and evaluation of infrastructure resilience, providing significant benefits for operators, planners, and policymakers. The paper discusses the theoretical underpinnings, detailed methodologies, and practical applications, offering insights into enhancing resilience against various operational challenges and external threats.

articleTitle: Intentional islanding method with temporary overvoltage analysis
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: As climate-related disasters become more frequent, enhancing the resilience of distribution systems and ensuring supply reliability have become critical tasks for many power utilities. One promising solution is intentional islanding utilizing distributed generation (DG). Through islanding, it is possible to continue supplying power to loads and reduce inconveniences during fault recovery procedures. However, additional faults can occur after forming an islanded system. In disaster situations, faults occur simultaneously and can happen with a time delay. In such cases, the islanded system must ensure robust operation by considering TOV (Temporary Overvoltage). If TOV is not controlled correctly, the islanded system may be exposed to overvoltage, leading to more significant damage. This paper introduces an islanding method that considers TOV. Furthermore, the methodology was applied to a modified IEEE 33-bus system to demonstrate its usefulness. Simulation results confirmed that TOV can be avoided through adjustments to GFL inverter-based DG without significantly impacting load supply.

articleTitle: Research on fault prediction and self-healing strategy of power distribution system based on big data analysis
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: In modern society, the power system, as one of the infrastructure, plays a vital role in human life and production. However, as an important part of the power system, the distribution system often faces a variety of faults and problems, which will not only lead to power supply interruption, but also may cause safety accidents and economic losses. Therefore, it is urgent to timely and accurately predict the failure of the distribution system and adopt effective self-healing strategies. This paper studies the fault prediction and self-healing strategy based on big data. First, using the RS-IA model, a new method can precisely locate the fault points of the distribution network. Secondly, the fault diagnosis and prediction model of the distribution network based on fuzzy integration is established. By mathematical description of fuzzy integration, the preliminary diagnosis results are pretreatment, the fuzzy metric is determined, and the high-precision fault prediction of the distribution network is realized. The experimental results show that the algorithm presented in is effective.

articleTitle: Resilience of electric distribution systems in Brazil: analysis of the regulatory framework and the ongoing project in the sector
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Electric distribution systems play a critical role in ensuring reliable power supply, particularly in regions susceptible to environmental and operational challenges. This article examines the resilience of electric systems in Brazil, focusing on preventive actions to be developed.

articleTitle: Quantifying distribution system resilience from utility data: large event risk and benefits of investments
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: We focus on large blackouts in electric distribution systems caused by extreme winds. Such events have a large cost and impact on customers. To quantify resilience to these events, we formulate large event risk and show how to calculate it from the historical outage data routinely collected by utilities’ outage management systems. Risk is defined using an event cost exceedance curve. The tail of this curve and the large event risk is described by the probability of a large cost event and the slope magnitude of the tail on a log-log plot. Resilience can be improved by planned investments to upgrade system components or speed up restoration. The benefits that these investments would have had if they had been made in the past can be quantified by "rerunning history" with the effects of the investment included, and then recalculating the large event risk to find the improvement in resilience. An example using utility data shows a 12% and 22% reduction in the probability of a large cost event due to 10% wind hardening and 10% faster restoration respectively. This new data-driven approach to quantify resilience and resilience investments is realistic and much easier to apply than complicated approaches based on modeling all the phases of resilience. Moreover, an appeal to improvements to past lived experience may well be persuasive to customers and regulators in making the case for resilience investments.

articleTitle: Renewable energy output control method to resolve electricity supply and demand imbalance
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: As interest in climate change increases globally, renewable energy connected to the power system has rapidly increased in accordance with the government's renewable energy supply plan and carbon neutrality policy. As a result, an imbalance in electricity supply and demand occurred due to an oversupply of renewable energy in areas with insufficient demand for electricity. To solve this problem, we would like to propose a method for remotely monitoring and controlling the output of renewable energy.

articleTitle: Technological roadmap for enhancing electric distribution resilience in Brazil: A framework for classifying extreme weather events
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This article aims to outline a technological and regulatory roadmap for Advanced Distribution Management Systems (ADMS) in Brazilian electricity distribution utilities to enhance the anticipation of extreme weather events and increase network resilience.

articleTitle: Outage prediction for extreme weather events based on machine learning
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Extreme weather-related events, such as hurricanes or winter storms pose significant challenges to the reliable operation of the power distribution networks, resulting in prolonged power outages, substantial economic repercussions, and threats to human wellbeing. Electric utility companies strive to minimize the severity of outages caused by such events, thus paving the way to a smooth post-event restoration and ensuring uninterrupted service delivery. In that context, advanced predictive analytics can enhance the network's resilience since knowing the expected outages prior to the event would allow network operators to protect critical areas. In this paper, we propose a tree-based, probabilistic machine-learning approach for outage prediction prior to extreme weather events. The method predicts the proportion of customers without power for a specified service territory based on weather forecasts, such as wind speed, air pressure, and precipitation. The algorithm is flexible and can be used for different prediction horizons, from few hours up to several days ahead. We test and validate the algorithm based on selected evaluation metrics using historical data of extreme weather events (hurricanes, heavy rainfall, nor’easter, and snowstorms) and outages in different U.S. counties. The presented results show stable prediction performance with high accuracy across different regions and events of different intensities.

articleTitle: Monitoring and system estimation tool for a hydro power plant in automated islanded grid operation for emergency power supply
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Intentional islanded grid operation utilizing local renewable generation units can significantly mitigate the impact of power failures. The LINDA 2.0 project demonstrates the feasibility of using an existing hydro power plant as an automated emergency power supply for critical loads. A tool is developed to assist the operator during the islanded operation of a Kaplan hydro power plant, enabling system estimation and monitoring functions. The tool serves as a crucial aid for operators in assessing system stability, e.g., ensuring that protection limits are not exceeded and thus preventing load loss and secure operation. Leveraging its monitoring and estimation capabilities, the tool increases the reliability of the emergency power supply and minimizes consequential damage by effective monitoring and alert management.

articleTitle: Electric power infrastructure exposure index for resilience studies
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Resilience studies focus on the capacity of geographical locations and population within to prepare for, respond to, recover from, and adapt to present and future loss-causing events. Depending on the discipline, resilience can find different definitions, however, all the definitions agree in the types of events that will impact the resilience of the system understudy: High-impact, low-frequency (HILF) risks. Recent work regarding the adoption of resilience indicators for planning in the power systems domain proposes modeling power system infrastructure risk using 4 indicators: Hazard, Exposure, Vulnerability and Response. These indicators focus on evaluating the possible causes and consequences of electrical infrastructure exposed to natural hazards or extreme events, helping to characterize the risk, and serving utilities for identifying the actions that need to be taken for mitigating the effects of such events. This paper centers on the exposure indicator, focusing on determining the presence of electric power system infrastructure in settings or places that could be adversely affected. This indicator considers all the possible events within a time range that can influence infrastructure’s health and availability. These events are modeled as weather forecasting in the form of geographical layers available to the public, such as the ones provided by the USDA Forest service, the National Land Cover Database, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), among others. These geographic layers describe the risk of natural disasters nationwide using map-based references with color coding depending on the weather threat and location.

articleTitle: A study on a multi-purpose ESS utilization business model for enhancing grid resilience
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: With the expansion of renewable energy and distributed power, the importance of introducing energy storage systems (ESS) as a flexible resource for stable power grid operation is increasing. ESS plays a key role in mitigating the variability of renewable energy, resolving issues with power grid construction delays, and achieving grid resilience and carbon neutrality. The ESS market is divided into 'FTM (In front of the meter)' market and 'BTM (Behind the meter)' market based on battery size, application, and installation location. To enhance grid resilience, expanding standalone grid-connected ESS in the FTM market is crucial. However, ESS remains expensive in the global market, and due to the high cost structure, securing profitability with ESS that performs fragmented functions is challenging. To address this issue, utilizing energy storage systems (ESS) for various purposes rather than a single role could be a solution. For example, it can be used for grid stabilization and customer peak reduction purposes. Therefore, in order to promote the widespread adoption of grid-connected ESS, it is essential to establish a business model that secures profitability and attracts investment from public and private sectors. Therefore, this paper aims to propose a new shared ESS model between FTM and BTM that reflects this, and to derive a new business model for grid-connected ESS through an analysis of the benefits for utilities, ESS Operators and participating customers.

articleTitle: Topographical assessment of electrical distribution system vulnerability to heavy rainfall events
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This paper presents a method for assessing the vulnerability of electrical distribution systems to heavy rainfall events, focusing on topographical factors such as surface runoffs and sinks. With geoinformatic analyses, the method evaluates the risks to electrical equipment in Germany. The key findings identify which medium voltage substations are potentially vulnerable. This method assesses and improves the resilience and reliability of electrical distribution systems in the face of climate change.

articleTitle: Benefits and use-cases of four-wire inverters for inverter-based DERs
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Most of today’s three-phase inverter-based distributed energy resources (DERs) utilize three-wire inverters that are designed and operated as balanced sources to minimize cost. Such inverters mainly inject balanced, positive-sequence current with very minimal negative-sequence current and no zero-sequence current. As a result, without grounding from interconnection transformer or a separate grounding bank, inverter-based DERs today do not provide a grounding path and have limited capability in supporting unbalanced loads and suppressing ground fault overvoltage. This paper introduces a less popular inverter topology for DERs: four-wire inverter and explores its benefits and use-cases for inverter-based DERs. Four-wire inverters can be realized through three-leg split DC link or four-leg configurations. They provide a neutral point and grounding/zero-sequence path for three-phase four-wire systems and can handle the neutral current due to unbalanced and/or nonlinear loads. Besides comparing the capability, performance, and cost of three-wire and four-wire inverters, the benefit of a four-wire grid-forming inverter in microgrid application is demonstrated using electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations. Specifically, its ability to provide sufficient grounding to reduce voltage unbalance during normal operation and to mitigate overvoltage during a single line-to-ground fault is presented. Moreover, how a four-wire grid-forming inverter can be potentially leveraged to simplify microgrid control, protection and grounding design and operation is discussed.

articleTitle: Forecasting needs for improving grid resilience in shore power infrastructures
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Energy transition is a major goal for humanity to mitigate climate change. Transportation is one of the sectors that should contribute the most to the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. Shore Side Energy is proposed as one of the main approaches to reduce the emissions of vessels when they are docked. Nevertheless, several improvements should be made in ports to achieve optimal management of energy, considering the needs of vessels. To achieve this goal, accurate forecasting tools need to be used. In the present paper, a forecasting framework to be used in ports is described, and some results are presented. The proposed framework will be used in a European project, Shift2DC.

articleTitle: Enhancing grid reliability: optimal allocation of DER for load support during contingencies
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This paper addresses the strategic allocation of distributed energy resources (DER) in the distribution network for enhancing grid reliability. The goal is to demonstrate that DER can be utilized to support system loads during contingencies, significantly increasing the network's resilience, since it's properly allocated. Through spatial analyses and electrical network modeling, areas suitable to receive DER were identified, considering factors such as losses due to the integration of distributed generation and variations in load voltage levels, with a focus on ensuring supply reliability and energy quality for consumers during contingencies cases.

articleTitle: Contribution of electric vehicle supply infrastructures based on DC microgrid to internal and grid-side resilience
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: The integration of electric vehicles into the distribution network represents a challenging aspect in the transport decarbonization process. EV supply infrastructures equipped with photovoltaic system, energy storage device and electric vehicle charging stations in DC configuration are shown to be flexible and viable solution to mitigate the impact of EV penetration. In this paper, a methodology for the assessment of the potential impact of DC-based electric vehicle supply infrastructures on microgrid and distribution network resilience improvements is proposed. In particular, the adopted approach aims at determining optimal day-ahead operation plan for microgrids to plan the possible contribution to grid-side active power reserve to cope with grid load forecast error or internal reserve to cover PV production uncertainty. A proper objective function to pursue techno-economic targets is defined, and the formulated optimization problem, based on mixed integer linear programming, accounts for technical constraints in a centralized manner. The proposed procedure is tested, with the technical features of a DC microgrid demonstrator, on a realistic distribution network.

articleTitle: Enhancing LV system resilience through probabilistic forecasting of interdependent variables: voltage, reactive and active power
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This paper presents a probabilistic forecasting approach tailored for low voltage (LV) substations, offering short-term predictions for three crucial variables: voltage, reactive power, and active power. These parameters play a vital role in the resilience of distribution systems, especially in the presence of Distributed Energy Resources (DERs). Evaluation with simulated data shows that active and reactive power forecasts degrade notably with higher EV penetration, whereas voltage forecasting experiences less degradation across all scenarios.

articleTitle: A new method for assessing grid resilience and power outages based on dynamic systems theory
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: One of the biggest challenges in managing power grids is maintaining a constant balance between supply and demand. Otherwise, the system will be destabilized, resulting in poor power quality or reaching a critical point where sudden power outages and other disruptions occur. Here we propose a new method for monitoring energy networks that can assess whether a network is approaching a critical point and requires special protection or is in a high resilience area. The central part of the analysis is the calculation of the Network Resilience Index (NRI) directly from the network voltage time series data. Mathematically, the index is based on bifurcation theory. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach by analyzing realistic simulations based on the Kuramoto model of coupled harmonic oscillators and show results for scenarios with grid failures caused by infrastructure degradation and extreme weather events.

articleTitle: Certified insulation systems for improving resilience of transformers and distribution grids
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This paper emphasizes the importance of insulation systems for grid resiliency and the certification processes that ensure their safety and reliability. Global standardization organizations and certification bodies have established evaluation methods to verify performance of insulation systems, which is becoming more important as newer insulation materials become more prevalent. Using a certified insulation system can support a more resilient grid by lessening the resources required for new equipment evaluation and enable faster deployment of transformers in times such as disaster. This paper also gives an example of a certified insulation system using advanced materials for liquid filled transformers and a compatibility evaluation – both supporting a more resilient grid.

articleTitle: Strategic load shedding for reduced impact of extreme weather events on distribution systems
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Extreme weather events such as heat/cold waves can create an imbalance between electricity generation and demand. In such events, utilities resort to several approaches for rebalancing supply and demand, the last one typically being load shedding through rotating outages at the substation/feeder level. Increasing communication and controllability provided by distribution automation and grid-edge smart meter devices creates the opportunity to shed loads in a strategic fashion. This paper presents and discusses innovative approaches for load shedding in distribution systems, highlighting their advantages and disadvantages. A simulation-based case study with a realistic synthetic model was performed to compare the performance of the discussed strategies.

articleTitle: Prosumer-enabled grid resillience – emerging systems view from pilots and vision for standards based interoperability
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: This paper discusses the importance of prosumer systems to ensure grid resilience in the wake of challenges posed by climate change and the rise in integration of intermittent energy resources on the grids, by securing energy supply, and support grid operations with demand side flexibility. We provide a snapshot of pilot projects and ongoing work in standard bodies, which will help to establish prosumer’s viability in grid resilience equation.

articleTitle: A framework for improving grid resilience by improving the reliability of load following services of microgrids
publicationTitle: CIRED Chicago Workshop 2024: Resilience of Electric Distribution Systems
abstract: Many energy-intensive industrial sectors are resorting to electrification to lower fossil fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions. Consequently, many industries will experience an increased need for electric energy, and many production sites will be installing large renewable energy production facilities, including batteries for energy storage. These new facilities will likely form industrial microgrids connected to the main distribution grid, which will be used to absorb fluctuations in renewable energy production, causing additional stress for grid operators. To help address those issues, this paper presents a two-layer stochastic optimization framework that provides day-ahead planning and intra-day bid following functionalities to microgrid, in presence of uncertainties.
